title: Agro-Biomass Biochars from Pyrolysis to Rhizosphere: Feedstock Controls, Carbon Stability, and Ecological Synergies
content: This study comprehensively evaluates the thermochemical valorization of agricultural residues into biochar, examining its integration into advanced closed-loop agro-ecological frameworks such as the plant-driven enhanced rock weathering (ERW) system (e.g., the Lupinus albus–basalt model). By classifying precursor biomass feedstocks into three primary categories—leguminous and specialty herbaceous residues, staple cereal straws and stalks, and lignocellulosic woody biomass and orchard prunings—the review investigates how biochemical composition and pyrolysis operational parameters (such as peak temperature, heating rate, and residence time) critically dictate solid mass recovery, structural porosity, Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC), and carbon stability. While leguminous and herbaceous residues yield nutrient-rich biochars with high inorganic alkalinity optimal for neutralizing soil acidity, cereal straws offer versatile porous networks suitable for soil conditioning and environmental remediation. Conversely, lignin-rich woody residues and orchard prunings provide exceptional environmental recalcitrance and multi-century mean residence times, making them premier candidates for permanent carbon sequestration, structural construction materials, and phase-change material encapsulation. The findings demonstrate that strategic feedstock selection and precise thermal control enable the design of bespoke biochars that simultaneously drive negative emission technologies, soil restoration, and circular bioeconomy pathways.
